title: Caching Activations Over a Dataset
description: Documentation for the nnsight Python library

toc.label: Two decisions that set the cost of the whole run
The anchor: does the cache still match the model?
Padding: the reduction that quietly includes pad positions
Using the data: where is duplicate-token detection computed?
Using the data: outlier dimensions over the corpus

segments.html:
Most interpretability work that goes past a single prompt starts the same way: run a corpus through a model, keep some activations, write them to disk, and then do something with them — train a probe, fit a dictionary, compute feature statistics. The modelling is the interesting part. The collection is where runs die: at hour three, at 40,000 of 50,000 sequences, out of memory, or — worse — quietly, with tensors on disk that no longer match the model that produced them.

This tutorial builds that collection step end to end on GPT-2 and a small slice of WikiText. It is sized to run in Colab, and structured so that the only thing that changes at 50,000 sequences is a constant. We will:

  • capture many modules per forward pass with tracer.cache(modules=[...]), and measure what an unfiltered cache costs;
  • wrap collection in torch.no_grad() and measure what forgetting costs;
  • shard to disk with a manifest, kill the run halfway, and resume it;
  • anchor the cache — re-run a random sample of rows and check the stored tensors match a fresh forward pass bit-for-bit — and then show the re-check that will never be bit-exact, so you don't chase it;
  • watch GPU memory across the whole run, because a leak that is invisible at 100 sequences is fatal at 50,000;
  • handle padding, which silently poisons every reduction over a variable-length batch;
  • and then actually use the data: a layer sweep that localises duplicate-token detection to attention layer 0, against a control that sits at exactly chance.

A cache that has drifted from the model is worse than no cache: everything downstream is wrong and nothing raises. Roughly half of this tutorial is the checks that keep that from happening.

segments.html:
The corpus

Two things make a corpus job easy that are easy to skip.

Pack, don't pad. We concatenate the tokenized text into one long stream and cut it into fixed-length blocks. Every row then has exactly SEQ_LEN real tokens, so there are no pad positions to mask, no attention-mask bookkeeping, and no ragged batches. This is what SAE and probing pipelines normally do. When you can't pack — because rows are semantic units, like chat turns — you get padding, and the section Padding below shows exactly how badly that bites.

Tokenize once, up front. Tokenization is CPU work and re-doing it inside the capture loop puts it on the critical path. GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257, so the whole corpus fits in uint16 — 128 KB per 1,000 sequences of 64 tokens.

We take 2,048 blocks of 64 tokens = 131,072 tokens. That is small on purpose; it takes seconds and the numbers extrapolate linearly, which we check at the end.

segments.code:
from datasets import load_dataset

SEQ_LEN = 64
N_SEQ = 2048

ds = load_dataset("Salesforce/wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="train")

need = N_SEQ * SEQ_LEN
buf = np.empty(need + 4096, dtype=np.uint16)
n, batch = 0, []

for row in ds:
    if len(row["text"]) < 40:            # skip blank lines and section headers
        continue
    batch.append(row["text"])
    if len(batch) == 256:
        for seq in model.tokenizer(batch)["input_ids"]:
            k = min(len(seq), len(buf) - n)
            buf[n:n + k] = np.asarray(seq[:k], dtype=np.uint16)
            n += k
        batch = []
        if n >= need:
            break

corpus = buf[:need].reshape(N_SEQ, SEQ_LEN)
clear_output()
print(f"corpus: {corpus.shape} {corpus.dtype} = {corpus.nbytes/1e3:.0f} kB on disk, "
      f"{corpus.size:,} tokens")
print(repr(model.tokenizer.decode(corpus[0])[:180]) + " ...")

Row 0 starts mid-sentence, which is the point of packing: blocks are windows into a token stream, not documents.

One batch, one cache

tracer.cache(modules=[...]) records the output of every listed module for the whole run, in one forward pass. It sits on the same path the interleaver already uses to deliver values, so there are no per-module hooks to register and unregister, and it observes values after any intervention you apply.

Two things to know before the first call:

  • Cache keys are module paths prefixed with model. — the Envoy you pass in as model.transformer.h[6] comes back as "model.transformer.h.6". Print cache.keys() once rather than guessing.
  • A transformers-5 decoder block's .output is a bare tensor, but attn.output is a tuple. Both appear in the same cache. Unwrap defensively.

segments.code:
# The modules we will collect for the rest of this notebook.
#   transformer.drop  -- dropout after wte + wpe, i.e. the embeddings (identity in eval)
#   h[0].attn, h[0].mlp -- the two sublayers of block 0, to see where a feature appears
#   h[0..11]          -- the residual stream after each block
MODULES = ([model.transformer.drop, model.transformer.h[0].attn, model.transformer.h[0].mlp]
           + [model.transformer.h[i] for i in range(model.config.n_layer)])

NAMES = (["model.transformer.drop", "model.transformer.h.0.attn", "model.transformer.h.0.mlp"]
         + [f"model.transformer.h.{i}" for i in range(model.config.n_layer)])

LABELS = ["embeddings", "attn.0", "mlp.0"] + [f"block {i}" for i in range(model.config.n_layer)]

BATCH = 32
ids = torch.from_numpy(corpus[:BATCH].astype(np.int64))

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace({"input_ids": ids}) as tracer:
        cache = tracer.cache(modules=MODULES, dtype=torch.float16)

print(list(cache.keys())[:5], "...")
print()
for name in ["model.transformer.drop", "model.transformer.h.0.attn", "model.transformer.h.6"]:
    out = cache[name].output
    kind = type(out).__name__
    shape = out[0].shape if isinstance(out, tuple) else out.shape
    print(f"{name:30s} {kind:7s} {tuple(shape)} {(out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out).dtype}"
          f" on {(out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out).device}")

segments.html: h.0.attn came back as a tuple and the blocks as bare tensors — in the same cache, from the same trace. Indexing a block's output with [0] (the old nnsight idiom) would silently hand you row 0 of the batch instead of the hidden states. One helper removes the hazard:

segments.code:
def unwrap(value):
    # Blocks return a tensor; attention returns a tuple. Take the hidden states either way.
    return value[0] if isinstance(value, tuple) else value

print(unwrap(cache["model.transformer.h.0.attn"].output).shape)

segments.html:
Note also that dtype=torch.float16 and the default device=torch.device("cpu") are applied on the way out of the trace. Halving on the way out halves both the PCIe traffic and the bytes on disk, and — we check this later — it is exactly equivalent to capturing in fp32 and calling .half() afterwards.

Two decisions that set the cost of the whole run

Before writing a pipeline, two flags decide whether it is viable. Both are easy to get wrong because both are silent when wrong: the run still finishes, it just costs several times more than it should.

Decision 1: always pass modules=.

tracer.cache() with no arguments caches every module in the model. For GPT-2 that is 151 modules — every Conv1D, every LayerNorm, every dropout, and lm_head, whose output is [batch, seq, 50257]. All of it is copied device-to-host on every call. Let's measure both, at the batch size the pipeline will actually use.

segments.text:
cache()                775.7 ms/batch   151 modules     925.4 MiB copied to host
cache(modules=[...])     57.2 ms/batch    15 modules      45.0 MiB copied to host

segments.html:
On the A6000 this notebook ran on: 776 ms and 925 MiB per batch unfiltered, 57 ms and 45 MiB filtered — about 14x the time and 20x the bytes, for 136 modules we will never read. Over the 64 batches of the pipeline below that is 50 seconds of pure copying instead of 4. The research run behind this tutorial measured ~3 GB of blocking device-to-host copy per call at batch 128; adding modules= took one collection loop from 5 minutes to 3 seconds. Cache the modules you will read, and nothing else.

Decision 2: wrap collection in torch.no_grad().

A trace is a normal forward pass, so it runs with autograd on unless you say otherwise. Every intermediate the backward pass would need is kept alive, and any activation you hold comes back carrying a live grad_fn that pins the graph behind it. .detach() after the fact does not help: the graph was already built during the forward.

    h = nnsight.save(model.transformer.h[6].output)
print(f"no torch.no_grad(): grad_fn={type(h.grad_fn).__name__}  requires_grad={h.requires_grad}  device={h.device}")

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace({"input_ids": ids}) as tracer:
        h = nnsight.save(model.transformer.h[6].output)
print(f"with torch.no_grad(): grad_fn={h.grad_fn}  requires_grad={h.requires_grad}")
del h
_ = gc.collect()

segments.html: That is the mechanism. Here is the price, measured on the same work — 256 sequences, 15 modules, everything moved to CPU and freed each batch:

segments.code:
import contextlib

def capture_pass(n_seq, grad):
    if CUDA:
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    reset_peak()
    ctx = contextlib.nullcontext() if grad else torch.no_grad()
    sync(); t0 = time.time()
    with ctx:
        for i in range(0, n_seq, BATCH):
            batch_ids = torch.from_numpy(corpus[i:i + BATCH].astype(np.int64))
            with model.trace({"input_ids": batch_ids}) as tracer:
                c = tracer.cache(modules=MODULES, dtype=torch.float16)
            stacked = torch.stack([unwrap(c[name].output) for name in NAMES])
            del c, stacked
    sync()
    return gpu_mib("peak"), n_seq * SEQ_LEN / (time.time() - t0)

peak_ng, tps_ng = capture_pass(256, grad=False)
peak_g,  tps_g  = capture_pass(256, grad=True)
print(f"torch.no_grad(): peak {peak_ng:7.1f} MiB   {tps_ng:8.0f} tok/s")
print(f"autograd on    : peak {peak_g:7.1f} MiB   {tps_g:8.0f} tok/s")
print(f"                 -> {peak_g/max(peak_ng,1e-9):.2f}x peak memory, "
      f"{tps_ng/tps_g:.2f}x throughput")

segments.text:
torch.no_grad(): peak  1026.3 MiB      26464 tok/s
autograd on    : peak  3050.6 MiB      35450 tok/s
                 -> 2.97x peak memory, 0.75x throughput

segments.html:
~3x peak GPU memory — 1.0 GiB with no_grad, 3.0 GiB without.

Trust the memory ratio and not the throughput ratio. Peak allocation is deterministic and reproduced to the tenth of a MiB across runs; the timing is noise on a shared GPU, and across two runs of this notebook it came out 1.4x slower with autograd once and marginally faster the next time. The reason the time penalty is small at all is that we move each batch to the host and free it, so the graph is discarded every batch instead of accumulating — a pipeline that holds saved GPU tensors pays far more (earlier measurements on that shape put it near 18x memory and 11x time).

Either way, 3.0 GiB versus 1.0 GiB is the difference between fitting your batch size on the GPU and not, and nothing in the run hints that you are paying for gradients you will never use. Note that .detach() on the captured tensor does not help — tracer.cache(detach=True) is already the default, and the memory above was measured with it. The graph is built during the forward pass; only torch.no_grad() stops that.

tracer.cache() versus per-module .save()

You can write the same capture by hand: read each module's .output inside the trace, move it, and save the list. Is one faster? Let's interleave A/B/A/B so drift on a shared GPU doesn't decide the answer.

segments.code:
BLOCKS = [model.transformer.h[i] for i in range(model.config.n_layer)]
BLOCK_NAMES = [f"model.transformer.h.{i}" for i in range(model.config.n_layer)]
N_BENCH = 512

def run_cache():
    reset_peak(); sync(); t0 = time.time()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(0, N_BENCH, BATCH):
            b = torch.from_numpy(corpus[i:i + BATCH].astype(np.int64))
            with model.trace({"input_ids": b}) as tracer:
                c = tracer.cache(modules=BLOCKS, dtype=torch.float16)
            stacked = torch.stack([c[name].output for name in BLOCK_NAMES]); del c, stacked
    sync(); return N_BENCH * SEQ_LEN / (time.time() - t0), gpu_mib("peak")

def run_save():
    reset_peak(); sync(); t0 = time.time()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(0, N_BENCH, BATCH):
            b = torch.from_numpy(corpus[i:i + BATCH].astype(np.int64))
            with model.trace({"input_ids": b}) as tracer:
                hs = nnsight.save([blk.output.to("cpu", torch.float16) for blk in BLOCKS])
            stacked = torch.stack(hs); del hs, stacked
    sync(); return N_BENCH * SEQ_LEN / (time.time() - t0), gpu_mib("peak")

run_cache(); run_save()          # warm up, then interleave
for _ in range(3):
    (tc, pc), (ts, ps) = run_cache(), run_save()
    print(f"cache  {tc:8.0f} tok/s  peak {pc:7.1f} MiB   |   "
          f"save  {ts:8.0f} tok/s  peak {ps:7.1f} MiB")

segments.html:
Throughput and peak memory are the same to within run-to-run noise, and the tensors are identical. The choice is about ergonomics, not cost:

  • .save() keeps the move explicit — you write .to("cpu", torch.float16) yourself, so you can see exactly what crosses the bus and when. It also requires you to know which modules return tuples.
  • tracer.cache() wins when you don't want to hard-code module names, when you want inputs as well as outputs (include_inputs=True), and above all in a generation loop, where it appends one entry per decoding step automatically instead of needing a per-step save.

One flag is worth knowing about even though we do not pass it. tracer.cache(...) copies synchronously by default (non_blocking=False). non_blocking=True enqueues the device-to-host copy and returns immediately; nothing synchronises before you read the result, and reading a CPU tensor does not synchronise CUDA, so you can read a tensor whose copy is still in flight. It fails silently, it fails worse under GPU contention, and it is how a whole shard set becomes garbage. Leave the default alone unless you synchronise yourself.

The pipeline

Now the real thing. The design is four decisions, and none of them are nnsight's job — which is the point: nothing global survives a trace, so a capture loop is just a loop.

Step 1: shard. Write every SHARD_SEQ sequences to their own file. Shards are the unit of resumption, the unit of parallel reading later, and they keep peak host memory to one shard rather than the whole corpus.

Step 2: write atomically. torch.save to shard_0007.pt.tmp, then os.replace it onto shard_0007.pt. os.replace is atomic within a filesystem, so a file with the final name is always complete. A kill -9 mid-write leaves a .tmp that the next run ignores.

Step 3: keep a manifest. One JSON line per completed shard — index, filename, byte count, and which corpus rows it holds — flushed and fsynced. On restart we trust a shard only if the manifest lists it and the file on disk is exactly the recorded size.

Step 4: log memory per shard. Allocated, peak and reserved GPU memory at every shard boundary. This costs nothing and it is the only way to distinguish "we are fine" from "we are 4% into the leak".

Store the token ids alongside the activations. Labels for probing come from the token stream, and a shard that cannot say which tokens it came from is much less useful later.

# Works at 100 sequences. Do not run this at 50,000.
all_acts = []
for i in range(0, N_SEQ, BATCH):
    batch_ids = torch.from_numpy(corpus[i:i + BATCH].astype(np.int64))
    with model.trace({"input_ids": batch_ids}) as tracer:
        cache = tracer.cache()                       # every module
    all_acts.append({k: cache[k].output for k in cache.keys()})
torch.save(all_acts, "acts.pt")

children.html: Four problems, in increasing order of how much they hurt: it caches every module (Decision 1); it runs with autograd on (Decision 2); it holds the entire corpus in host RAM before a single byte reaches disk; and if anything fails at sequence 49,000 — an OOM, a preempted node, a full disk — there is nothing on disk to resume from.

segments.code:
def capture_batch(batch_ids):
    # One forward pass -> {module name: [batch, seq, hidden] fp16 on the host}.
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace({"input_ids": batch_ids}) as tracer:
            cache = tracer.cache(modules=MODULES, dtype=torch.float16)
    return {name: unwrap(cache[name].output) for name in NAMES}


def write_shard(out_dir, index, payload, rows):
    # Atomic write + one fsync'd manifest line. Never leaves a half-written shard.
    fname = f"shard_{index:04d}.pt"
    tmp = os.path.join(out_dir, fname + ".tmp")
    torch.save(payload, tmp)
    os.replace(tmp, os.path.join(out_dir, fname))          # atomic within a filesystem
    nbytes = os.path.getsize(os.path.join(out_dir, fname))
    with open(os.path.join(out_dir, "manifest.jsonl"), "a") as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps({"shard": index, "file": fname, "bytes": nbytes,
                             "rows": [int(rows[0]), int(rows[-1]) + 1]}) + "\n")
        fh.flush()
        os.fsync(fh.fileno())


def completed_shards(out_dir):
    # Shards the manifest claims AND whose file is present at the recorded size.
    done = {}
    manifest = os.path.join(out_dir, "manifest.jsonl")
    if os.path.exists(manifest):
        for line in open(manifest):
            record = json.loads(line)
            path = os.path.join(out_dir, record["file"])
            if os.path.exists(path) and os.path.getsize(path) == record["bytes"]:
                done[record["shard"]] = record
    return done

segments.html:
Shard 7 is in the manifest but is 4 kB short, so the size check rejects it and it will be rewritten. The .tmp file is never a candidate, because only files with the final name are ever considered. This is the whole of resumability: about twenty lines, none of them nnsight-specific.

Re-running the identical call now picks up where it stopped.

segments.html:
Seven shards were skipped (0–6), and shards 7–15 were written — shard 7 because we truncated it. Note what did not happen: no global state carried over from the crashed run, no cache had to be invalidated, and the resumed segment needed no special code path.

The throughput number is end-to-end and includes writing ~2.8 GiB to disk, which for this module list is the dominant cost — 15 modules at fp16 is 1.4 MiB of activations per sequence, or about 22 kB per token. Capture without the disk writes ran at roughly 26,000 tok/s in the no_grad cell above; the writes are what you are paying for here, which is the usual shape of a corpus job once the module list is more than a layer or two.

segments.html:
This is why storage tiering matters at real scale. Sixty-nine gigabytes for 3.2M tokens is a lot of disk to fill before you know whether the experiment works. The pipeline this tutorial is derived from stored one layer token-level for all 50,000 sequences (4.6 GiB), per-layer pooled means for all 50,000 (0.9 GiB), and all layers token-level for only the first 4,096 (4.5 GiB) — 10.7 GiB total instead of 69. Decide which slice you need at full scale and which you only need a sample of, and store them separately.

Did anything leak?

The failure this section exists to prevent looks like this: the run is fine for an hour, then dies at 80%. Anything that accumulates per trace — a retained graph, an uncollected reference cycle, a growing list — is invisible over 100 prompts and fatal over 50,000. We logged memory at every shard boundary, so we can simply look.

segments.code:

fig = px.line(df, x="shard", y=["allocated", "peak", "reserved"], markers=True,
              labels={"value": "GPU memory (MiB)", "shard": "shard index",
                      "variable": ""},
              title="GPU memory at every shard boundary")
fig.update_yaxes(rangemode="tozero")
fig.show()

print("allocated:", df["allocated"].min(), "->", df["allocated"].max(), "MiB",
      f"(spread {df['allocated'].max() - df['allocated'].min():.3f} MiB)")
print("peak     :", df["peak"].min(), "->", df["peak"].max(), "MiB")

segments.html:
Three flat lines. Allocated memory at every shard boundary is identical to the byte (483.6 MiB — the model's weights and nothing else), and cumulative peak never moves off the first batch's high-water mark. Whatever the interleaver allocates per trace, it gives back before the next one; the del of each batch's captured tensors returns the rest.

This is the check to keep in your own pipeline, not because nnsight is suspect but because your accumulator usually is. A single results.append(tensor_still_on_gpu) shows up here as a straight line with a slope, hours before it shows up as an OOM.

The anchor: does the cache still match the model?

Everything above is bookkeeping. This is the check that makes the bookkeeping worth anything.

The activations went to the host, changed dtype, went through torch.save, and came back through torch.load. Any of those steps can quietly change values — a wrong dtype, a wrong row order, an off-by-one in a shard offset, an asynchronous copy read too early. None of it raises. So: draw a random sample of rows from across all the shards, reconstruct the batch they were captured in, run it again, and compare with torch.equal.

Reconstructing the batch is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters — see below.

segments.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sample_rows = np.sort(rng.choice(N_SEQ, 32, replace=False))
CHECK = "model.transformer.h.6"

# what we stored
stored = {}
for row in sample_rows:
    s = row // SHARD_SEQ
    shard = torch.load(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, f"shard_{s:04d}.pt"), weights_only=False)
    assert int(shard["rows"][row - s * SHARD_SEQ]) == row      # row bookkeeping is right
    stored[row] = shard["acts"][CHECK][row - s * SHARD_SEQ].clone()
    del shard

def fresh(batch_rows):
    batch_ids = torch.from_numpy(corpus[batch_rows].astype(np.int64))
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace({"input_ids": batch_ids}) as tracer:
            c = tracer.cache(modules=[model.transformer.h[6]], dtype=torch.float16)
    return c[CHECK].output

# re-run each sampled row inside the exact batch it was collected in
exact, worst = 0, 0.0
for row in sample_rows:
    start = (row // BATCH) * BATCH
    again = fresh(np.arange(start, start + BATCH))[row - start]
    exact += int(torch.equal(again, stored[row]))
    worst = max(worst, (again.float() - stored[row].float()).abs().max().item())

print(f"identical batch composition: {exact}/{len(sample_rows)} bit-exact, max abs diff {worst:g}")

segments.text: identical batch composition: 32/32 bit-exact, max abs diff 0

segments.html:
32 of 32, bit-for-bit, max absolute difference exactly zero. The shards on disk are the model's activations, not something that resembles them. Run this on every collection, on a sample from both ends of the run, and make it an assertion rather than a printout.

Now the trap. The obvious way to write this check is "take a few sampled rows, run them again, diff" — without reconstructing the original batch. That check never passes, and it is not a bug in your pipeline:

segments.code:
rows_out = []
for bs in (32, 16, 8, 4, 1):
    exact, worst, rel = 0, 0.0, []
    for i in range(0, len(sample_rows), bs):
        chunk = sample_rows[i:i + bs]
        again = fresh(chunk)
        for j, row in enumerate(chunk):
            exact += int(torch.equal(again[j], stored[row]))
            diff = (again[j].float() - stored[row].float()).abs()
            worst = max(worst, diff.max().item())
            rel.append((diff.mean() / stored[row].float().abs().mean()).item())
    rows_out.append({"re-run batch size": bs, "bit-exact": f"{exact}/{len(sample_rows)}",
                     "max abs diff": worst, "mean relative diff": float(np.mean(rel))})
pd.DataFrame(rows_out)

re-run batch size bit-exact max abs diff mean relative diff
0 32 32/32 0.00000 0.000000
1 16 32/32 0.00000 0.000000
2 8 0/32 0.03125 0.000001
3 4 0/32 0.03125 0.000001
4 1 0/32 0.03125 0.000001

Read that carefully, because it is more specific than "floating point is fuzzy".

The rows were collected in batches of 32. Re-running them as a batch of 32 — different rows, same shape — is bit-exact. So is a batch of 16. At batch 8 and below, nothing is bit-exact, with a max absolute difference around 3e-2 and a mean relative difference around 1e-6.

It is the batch shape, not the batch contents, that changes the answer: cuBLAS picks a different GEMM kernel for a different shape, and different kernels sum in a different order. That is torch, not nnsight — the same thing happens with plain register_forward_hook. Two consequences:

  • A validation script that asserts bit-equality on re-batched samples will fail forever and teach its author nothing. Reconstruct the batch, or compare with a tolerance (torch.allclose(..., atol=1e-2) at fp16) and say so out loud.
  • Numbers computed from a cache are reproducible at the batch shape the cache was built at. Record the batch size in your manifest alongside the model name, dtype and revision.

One more round-trip worth checking: does dtype=torch.float16 in the cache mean anything different from capturing in fp32 and halving afterwards?

start = (row // BATCH) * BATCH

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace({"input_ids": batch_ids}) as tracer:
        c32 = tracer.cache(modules=[model.transformer.h[6]], dtype=None)   # keep fp32
print("captured dtype:", c32[CHECK].output.dtype)
print("fp32 capture then .half()  ==  cache(dtype=float16):",
      torch.equal(c32[CHECK].output.half()[row - start], stored[row]))

fp32 capture then .half()  ==  cache(dtype=float16): True

segments.html:
Identical. The cast is a post-hoc .half(), so storing fp16 costs nothing in fidelity relative to casting yourself — it halves disk and PCIe for free. (What fp16 costs relative to fp32 storage is a separate question, and it is the usual one: ~1e-3 relative precision, fine for probes and dictionary learning, not fine if you plan to take differences of nearly equal activations.)

Padding: the reduction that quietly includes pad positions

Our corpus is packed, so every position is real. As soon as your rows are semantic units of different lengths — prompts, chat turns, documents you refuse to split — the batch is padded and every reduction over it is wrong unless you mask.

nnsight sets tokenizer.padding_side = "left" when it loads the model, so tokenizing the prompts yourself reproduces exactly the batch a list of strings would have produced — and hands you the attention_mask, which you need anyway.

segments.code:
prompts = [
    "Hello world.",
    "The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of",
    "In 1969, humans first walked on the surface of the Moon, an event watched by",
    "Cats sleep.",
    "A quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog while the sun sets behind distant hills and the river",
]
enc = model.tokenizer(prompts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
mask = enc["attention_mask"]
print("padding side:", model.tokenizer.padding_side, "| batch:", tuple(enc["input_ids"].shape))
print("pad positions per row:", (mask == 0).sum(1).tolist())

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(enc) as tracer:
        c = tracer.cache(modules=[model.transformer.h[6]], dtype=torch.float16)
acts = c[CHECK].output.float()

norms = acts.norm(dim=-1)
print(f"\nmean activation norm at pad positions : {norms[mask == 0].mean():8.1f}")
print(f"mean activation norm at real positions: {norms[mask == 1].mean():8.1f}")

Using the data: where is duplicate-token detection computed?

A pipeline is only validated when something downstream works. We ask a question the cache is well suited to answer and a single prompt is not: at what depth does GPT-2 represent "this token has already appeared in this window"?

The property is a good test case. Labels are free — read them off the token stream — and it cannot be computed from a single token's identity: it depends on the rest of the context, so a model has to move information between positions to represent it. If it appears somewhere, attention put it there.

The confound is severe, and it is worth stating before we touch the activations. Both the token's identity and its position predict repetition on their own: common tokens repeat more, and later positions have more preceding tokens to repeat (0.3% repeats at position 1, 37% at position 63). The embedding layer knows both. So a probe that reads 0.98 at layer 0 may have learned nothing about duplication at all.

Our control is a matched design: we keep pairs of examples with the same (position, token id), one repeated and one not. Within any such pair the embedding is identical by construction, so position and token identity carry exactly zero information about the label, and anything a probe reads must have come from context.

segments.code:
tokens = corpus.astype(np.int64)

# label: has this exact token id occurred earlier in this 64-token window?
repeat = np.zeros_like(tokens, dtype=bool)
for i in range(N_SEQ):
    seen = set()
    for t in range(SEQ_LEN):
        repeat[i, t] = tokens[i, t] in seen
        seen.add(tokens[i, t])

print(f"repeat rate overall: {repeat.mean():.3f}")
print(f"  at position  1: {repeat[:, 1].mean():.3f}")
print(f"  at position 63: {repeat[:, 63].mean():.3f}   <- position alone predicts the label")

If the matching worked, a classifier that sees only the position, or only the token id, must sit at chance — and not just on held-out data, but even when we let it fit and score the same training set, which is an upper bound on anything it could extract.

segments.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning

# lbfgs is capped at 100 iterations on purpose: it keeps the 15-layer sweep to a couple of
# minutes, and every accuracy below is within 0.005 of the same fit at max_iter=1000.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=ConvergenceWarning)

def probe(X_train, y_tr, X_test, y_te, max_iter=100):
    mu, sd = X_train.mean(0, keepdims=True), X_train.std(0, keepdims=True) + 1e-6
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=max_iter).fit((X_train - mu) / sd, y_tr)
    return clf.score((X_test - mu) / sd, y_te)

pos_test = np.eye(SEQ_LEN, dtype=np.float32)[test_ex[:, 1]]

      f"(fit and scored on train: {probe(pos_train, y_train, pos_train, y_train):.4f})")

vocab = sorted(set(tokens[train_ex[:, 0], train_ex[:, 1]].tolist())
               | set(tokens[test_ex[:, 0], test_ex[:, 1]].tolist()))
index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vocab)}
tok_train = np.eye(len(vocab), dtype=np.float32)[[index[v] for v in tokens[train_ex[:, 0], train_ex[:, 1]]]]
tok_test = np.eye(len(vocab), dtype=np.float32)[[index[v] for v in tokens[test_ex[:, 0], test_ex[:, 1]]]]
print(f"token id only : test {probe(tok_train, y_train, tok_test, y_test):.4f}   "
      f"(fit and scored on train: {probe(tok_train, y_train, tok_train, y_train):.4f})")

Now we need the features. This is the part the cache exists for: one streaming pass over the shards, pulling only the (sequence, position) cells our example set names, for all fifteen modules at once. Loading each shard once and taking everything you need from it is the difference between a 1-second gather and re-reading 2.8 GiB fifteen times.

segments.code:
def gather(examples):
    # Stream the shards once -> {module name: [n_examples, hidden] fp16}.
    hidden = model.config.n_embd
    X = {name: np.zeros((len(examples), hidden), dtype=np.float16) for name in NAMES}
    t0 = time.time()
    for s in range(N_SEQ // SHARD_SEQ):
        which = np.where((examples[:, 0] >= s * SHARD_SEQ)
                         & (examples[:, 0] < (s + 1) * SHARD_SEQ))[0]
        if len(which) == 0:
            continue
        shard = torch.load(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, f"shard_{s:04d}.pt"), weights_only=False)
        rows, positions = examples[which, 0] - s * SHARD_SEQ, examples[which, 1]
        for name in NAMES:
            X[name][which] = shard["acts"][name][rows, positions].numpy()
        del shard
    print(f"gathered {len(examples):,} examples x {len(NAMES)} modules in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")
    return X

X_train, X_test = gather(train_ex), gather(test_ex)

segments.html:
The curve reads cleanly:

  • Embeddings: 0.5000. Not "near chance" — exactly chance, and the fit converges in zero iterations, because the matched design made wte[token] + wpe[position] identical within every pair. The baseline is dead by construction, and that is what makes the rest attributable.
  • attn.0: 0.945. One attention sublayer — the very first thing in the network that can move information between positions — takes the feature from provably absent to almost perfectly linearly decodable. This is where duplicate-token detection is computed.
  • mlp.0 0.972, block 0 0.970, block 1 0.977 (peak). The rest of block 0 and block 1 sharpen it a little; nothing else creates it.
  • Then a monotone decay to 0.707 at block 11. The information does not vanish — the model still uses it — but it stops being linearly readable as it is folded into representations for downstream computation. A layer sweep that only looked at the last block would have concluded the feature is weak.
  • Shuffled labels: 0.49–0.52 everywhere. The pipeline is not manufacturing signal.

This matches what is known about GPT-2 small from the IOI work: its duplicate-token heads live in attention layer 0 (and L3H0), well before the induction heads at layer 5. We recovered that from 2,048 windows of WikiText and a linear probe, with no prompt engineering — which is the argument for collecting activations over a corpus in the first place.

Using the data: outlier dimensions over the corpus

A second use, and a second kind of validation. Streaming statistics over every cached token is the cheapest way to ask whether the cache is a faithful sample of the model, because the answer is already known from the literature: GPT-2's residual stream has a small number of "rogue" dimensions with enormous magnitudes.

segments.code:
hidden = model.config.n_embd
n_tok, s1, s2 = 0, torch.zeros(hidden, dtype=torch.float64), torch.zeros(hidden, dtype=torch.float64)
dim_max = torch.zeros(hidden)

t0 = time.time()
for s in range(N_SEQ // SHARD_SEQ):
    x = torch.load(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, f"shard_{s:04d}.pt"),
                   weights_only=False)["acts"][CHECK].float().reshape(-1, hidden)
    n_tok += x.shape[0]
    s1 += x.sum(0).double()
    s2 += (x * x).sum(0).double()
    dim_max = torch.maximum(dim_max, x.abs().max(0).values)

mean = (s1 / n_tok).float()
std = ((s2 / n_tok).float() - mean ** 2).clamp(min=0).sqrt()
rms = (s2.sum() / (n_tok * hidden)).sqrt().item()
print(f"{n_tok:,} token vectors streamed in {time.time() - t0:.1f}s")
print(f"residual-stream RMS {rms:.2f}, median per-dimension max {dim_max.median():.2f}")

top = dim_max.argsort(descending=True)[:6].tolist()
pd.DataFrame([{"dim": d, "max |x|": round(dim_max[d].item(), 1), "mean": round(mean[d].item(), 2),
               "std": round(std[d].item(), 2), "max / RMS": round((dim_max[d] / rms).item(), 1)}
              for d in top])

Two of 768 dimensions stand out by more than an order of magnitude — 447 (max 3018, 213x the residual-stream RMS) and 138 (829). These are exactly the GPT-2 rogue dimensions reported in the outlier/massive-activation literature, recovered here from 131,072 cached tokens in a 1.5-second streaming pass. Finding them is an independent check that the cache is a faithful sample of the model, and it explains the padding result above: those dimensions live on the attention-sink positions, which is why pad positions had 8.6x the norm of real ones.

It is also a warning for anything you normalise: computing per-dimension statistics for an SAE, or whitening, over a corpus that includes pad positions will be driven by these two dimensions on positions that mean nothing.

Cleaning up

Shards are large and disposable — the pipeline regenerates them from the corpus and the model in a fixed amount of time. Delete them when the analysis is done, and never commit them.

Limitations

  • The corpus is 2,048 sequences. Everything scales linearly in tokens, and we printed the extrapolation, but a 34-minute 50,000-sequence run has failure modes a 20-second run does not: a filesystem that fills up, a preempted node, a dataloader that outruns the GPU. The shard/manifest/resume structure is what makes those survivable; it is not tested here at the scale it is for.
  • One model, one dtype, one device. All numbers are GPT-2 small in fp32 on one CUDA device. The ratios (unfiltered vs filtered cache, autograd vs no_grad) should carry; the absolute throughput will not. Multi-GPU or sharded models add a device dimension to every capture that this notebook does not cover.
  • Bit-exactness is a same-machine, same-shape claim. The anchor confirms the cache matches a fresh forward pass in this process, at this batch shape. Across GPU architectures, torch versions, or attention implementations, expect small differences and compare with a tolerance.
  • The probe measures linear decodability, not use. 0.945 at attn.0 says the information is there and linearly available; it does not show the model uses it downstream. The decay to 0.707 at block 11 is likewise about a linear reader, not about the information being destroyed. Establishing use requires an intervention — patch or ablate the layer-0 attention output and measure a behavioural effect.
  • Duplicate-token detection is one feature, chosen because it is cheap to label. The matched-pair control kills position and token identity; it does not rule out every correlate of repetition (for instance, whether the window is repetitive overall).
  • fp16 storage is a deliberate 2x saving that costs ~1e-3 relative precision. For probing and dictionary learning that is invisible; for differences of nearly equal activations it is not.

What to take with you

A checklist, in the order the failures happen:

  1. tracer.cache(modules=[...]) — always pass modules=. An unfiltered cache copies every module in the model to the host on every call.
  2. with torch.no_grad(): around read-only collection. ~3x peak GPU memory otherwise, with no warning and no error. .detach() afterwards does not undo it.
  3. Pack the corpus if you can; mask by attention_mask if you can't. Pad positions carry the largest activations in the batch, so an unmasked mean can be off by 300%.
  4. Shard, write to .tmp then os.replace, and keep an fsync'd manifest with byte counts. Twenty lines, and the run becomes restartable.
  5. Log allocated GPU memory per shard. Flat is the only acceptable shape.
  6. Anchor the cache: re-run a random sample in its original batch and assert torch.equal. Anything else — re-batched, re-ordered, batch of one — will differ in the last bits, because batch shape selects the kernel.
  7. Record the batch size, dtype, model revision and module list next to the data. They are what makes the numbers reproducible.
